transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2027-09-14 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Lena (Sable Platform), Tom (SRE), Priya (ML Infra)

Auto-summary (auto generated, may be incomplete): recurring eviction during mixed short/long requests; possible KV slot fragmentation; prefetch behavior interacting with batched callers; plan to gather traces and run a quantized dedicated benchmark.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): cool, hey everyone, thanks for joining. can you hear me okay?
[00:04] Lena (Sable): yeah, loud and clear. thanks for setting this up. we've been seeing latency spikes and token regen loops during mid-day bursts.
[00:12] Diego (Redwood SE): hi all — i'll focus on the runtime traces and kv playback, maya i'll help with the deck and the pilot discussion.
[00:19] Tom (SRE): quick context — Sable runs mixed short queries (single-turn search) and long-context chat sessions for support transcripts. the issue shows up when long-context requests rise above ~30% of stream; then eviction cascades and some sessions see degraded quality.
[00:35] Priya (ML Infra): and to add, we've noticed the tokenization and prefix patterns look... uh, somewhat correlated to certain user flows — repeated prefixes early in the chat.

[01:02] Diego: ok let's start with what the runtime shows. our KV is slot-based, we group prefixes into context-slots and try to maintain a working set. eviction happens when the in-memory KV slab approaches the high watermark. but what we're seeing in your telemetry is fragmentation — small free slots scattered across slabs which prevents large contiguous prefix writes, and a lot of paging to disk.
[01:35] Lena: can you explain the fragmentation term? is it about many small prefixes or something lower-level?
[01:40] Diego: good question. fragmentation here is twofold: logical fragmentation (prefixes that don't align to the same hot bucket so we can't reuse their cached embeddings efficiently) and physical fragmentation within the slab allocator — frequent allocate/deallocate of different sized prefix blobs leaves gaps. over time those gaps become unusable for new long-context tokens, so the runtime evicts older but still useful prefixes to make room, which increases misses.
[02:12] Tom: hmm that matches our heap charts — free bytes fragmented even though total free looks non-zero. we also saw spiky async disk reads (paging).

[02:30] Maya: is this something the model quantization choices affect? Priya?
[02:35] Priya: yes, quantization does change memory layout. int8 reduces base weight memory dramatically, but intermediate KV encodings and alignment can change. also some optimized kernels pack tensors differently; that packing can increase or decrease the effective prefix blob size — so it's non-linear.

[03:01] Diego: exactly. in some customers we've seen that when switching to a quantized int8 path, the runtime's slab allocator ends up with larger average allocation unit due to packing and low-level alignment, which reduces the number of per-slot allocations but increases average slot size — that sometimes reduces fragmentation, sometimes increases it depending on the prefix size distribution.
[03:27] Lena: interesting. so switching to int8 could help or hurt? we were considering int8 to reduce costs.
[03:33] Diego: yep, it's workload dependent. that's why our recommended medium-term playbook includes an int8 benchmark using your real prompt set. today we agreed we'll run that.

[03:52] Tom: what about prefetching — I think our team enabled aggressive prefetch heuristics last month to try to reduce cold misses, maybe that backfired?
[03:59] Diego: good call. prefetch is designed to pull likely next-prefixes into memory during generation, but with bursty mixed traffic it can create temporary hotspots. if a prefetch pattern loads many unique prefixes quickly, they consume contiguous space and then age out, leaving behind fragmentation when the long-context requests need contiguous chunks. so aggressive prefetch + small slab granularity = fragmentation amplifier.

[04:35] Priya: we also saw backpressure on the batching layer — some batches were being drained slowly because KV misses force recomputation. that amplified token latency which then changed downstream batching behavior.

[04:55] Diego: yep, there's a feedback loop. misses -> recompute -> longer batch processing -> larger queue -> more concurrent prefetches -> more allocations -> more eviction. nasty.

[05:16] Maya: okay, high-level mitigations? short, medium, long?

[05:22] Diego: short term (1-2 days): 1) relax the LRU eviction aggressiveness by increasing the free watermark threshold so we leave more headroom; 2) temporarily disable the most aggressive prefetch policy (the "speculative next-k" path) and put it to conservative mode; 3) route long-context sessions to nodes with larger KV slabs (we can do routing by header or route key). these reduce churn quickly.
[06:00] Tom: can you change routing with our Private/VPC setup? any network constraints?
[06:05] Diego: yes, with Redwood Private you can configure routing policies in the control plane and set capacity tags on nodes. for VPC we'll need the sidecar or router rules — Diego: note, sidecar env var KV_SLOT_TARGET can be used. (murmur)

[06:28] Lena: medium term (2-4 weeks)?
[06:31] Diego: medium: 1) run the int8 dedicated benchmark with your prompt set to see slab behavior and prefetch interactions; 2) introduce prefix bucketing — group prefixes by high-level fingerprint to increase reuse and reduce cross-bucket allocation; 3) implement an adaptive prefetch heuristic tied to current slab occupancy (pre-fetch aggressiveness decays as occupancy increases). this reduces hot churn.

[07:10] Priya: prefix bucketing sounds promising. is that safe for our privacy constraints? we have a legal requirement not to persist raw prompts beyond short windows.
[07:18] Diego: yes — bucketing uses a non-reversible fingerprint (sha256 truncated + salt) and only stores the fingerprint index, not raw text. it complies with the retention constraints — but we'll provide the exact design and a compliance note.

[07:40] Maya: long term?
[07:42] Diego: long term: 1) slab compaction background job — a controlled defragmenter that compacts and rebuilds live slab pages during low-load windows; 2) checkout hybrid eviction policies (LRU+frequency weighting) tuned by access patterns; 3) instrument more fine-grained telemetry like per-prefix allocation size histograms and contiguous free-run length to detect fragmentation before it causes paging.

[08:20] Tom: do we risk throughput regressions with compaction?
[08:24] Diego: compaction is throttled and runs during off-peak, but there is a tail risk — we propose a canary run on a small subset of nodes first.

[08:40] Speaker 1 (softly, unclear): is there a way to reduce the memory overhead without changing slab behavior, like different quantization or kernel choices?
[08:49] Priya: we can test alternative kernels — some kernels avoid packing and produce smaller allocation footprints at slight latency cost. also hybrid quantization (mixed int8 for weights + fp16 for attention KV) sometimes gives a sweet spot.

[09:20] Diego: worth noting: batching interacts — if you raise batch size to hide latency, you also increase peak KV working set because multiple tokens across different prefixes are served together. for Sable's traffic profile, we saw a sweet spot at batch 16 for warm workloads and batch 8 for mixed long-context. we'll surface the measured curves in the benchmark report.

[09:55] Lena: about our on-prem constraints: we can't ship raw logs off-site. can Redwood run traces in a privacy-preserving way?
[10:02] Maya: yes — we support two options: 1) shim that redacts prompt content and only exports fingerprints + allocation metadata; 2) run an on-call remote debugging session where you're comfortable sharing ephemeral logs in a signed ephemeral container. Diego will provide the steps.

[10:24] Diego: action: i'll share a kv-verbose trace capture script. it toggles full trace for a 15-minute window and redacts content, producing allocation tables, prefetch events, and slab maps. we'll include a sample where we annotate fragmentation spikes.

[10:45] Tom: good. one more question — we had one incident where the runtime paged to local SSD and hit high iowait; is that classic eviction/paging or something else?
[10:55] Diego: classic but with threshold caveats. when we hit the high watermark the runtime will asynchronously spill older prefixes to disk; if the spill rate outpaces background flushes and disk is slow (low IOPS), reads for those spilled prefixes cause high iowait. also simultaneous compaction/GC on the host can amplify.

[11:24] Priya: that incident co-occurred with a nightly backup job — disk contention was probably the multiplier.

[11:36] Maya: so to prevent iowait spikes short-term we should throttle spills or blacklist local backup windows?
[11:42] Diego: yes throttle spills and coordinate maintenance windows. we can also configure a spill-to-remote-store policy (object store) rather than local SSD if your infra allows it. that moves latency off the node.

[12:02] Lena: let's talk about the live demo you mentioned. what will Redwood run during the benchmark?
[12:06] Maya: the benchmark will run your provided prompt set across three configurations: hosted optimized fp16 baseline, Dedicated + int8 quantized, and Dedicated + fp16 with compaction enabled. we'll measure end-to-end P95/P99 lat, KV miss rate, spill rate, and token cost.

[12:28] Diego: and we'll capture per-prefix allocation histograms and prefetch event timelines so you can see how bucketing affects reuse.

[12:36] Tom: how long does the benchmark run?
[12:38] Diego: typically 2-4 hours to capture diurnal patterns; we can compress for a shorter window but risk missing high-variance events.

[12:50] Priya: okay we'll try for a 4 hour run during your next mid-day peak and set kv-verbose for a 15 minute window inside that.

[13:05] Lena: any quick config flags we can try immediately? you mentioned KV_SLOT_TARGET earlier. what else?
[13:11] Diego: flags: KV_SLOT_TARGET (target slots per slab), KV_EVICT_MARGIN (percent above watermark to avoid immediate eviction), PREFETCH_MODE (conservative/speculative), PREFETCH_BACKOFF (ms). we'll share recommended tuning values for your traffic.

[13:32] Speaker 2 (murmur): okay thanks.

[13:45] Maya: let's address a few troubleshooting heuristics — why you see prefix reuse drop even when user behavior hasn't changed. one is header hashing skew: if routing keys aren't stable, requests for same user can land on different node groups so they miss local KV. second is batch-induced eviction where many short requests in a batch evict prefixes tied to a long-context session.

[14:08] Tom: we do use consistent hashing on user_id, but we did change the routing header last sprint for experimentation. could that be it?

[14:14] Diego: yes, that would explain sudden drop in local hit-rate. easiest check: compute per-node hot prefix lists and see if an identical user_id maps to different nodes in the window. Diego: we'll include a script.

[14:30] Priya: any recommended guardrails for the consistency change?

[14:33] Diego: roll with sticky routing keys for sessions, and have a small global cache for cross-node hot prefix replication for a tiny set of super-hot prefixes. this reduces cross-node misses with low overhead.

[14:54] Lena: can we replicate the problem in a staging environment? we have limited capacity in staging though.

[15:00] Maya: Redwood can simulate the traffic pattern in a benchmark harness and emulate slab occupancies. for full-scale we'd recommend a short Dedicated pilot with identical CPU/GPU shapes.

[15:12] Diego: also note that some older kernels in the runtime had a bug where the free-run detector misreported contiguous free ranges resulting in premature compaction triggers; make sure your nodes run runtime >= 3.2.1 which includes a fix.

[15:34] Tom: we are on 3.1.8 right now. ok will plan upgrade. any risk with upgrade?

[15:40] Diego: minor — we recommend canary 10% nodes first. the fix is non-breaking but compaction timing changed.

[15:52] Lena: you mentioned hot-prefix index earlier — what does that look like and how big is it?

[15:57] Diego: it's a lightweight in-memory bloom + fingerprint table for the top N prefixes, N tunable (default 10k). memory cost is tens of megabytes and it dramatically reduces redundant prefetch. we can tune N per node.

[16:18] Priya: show of hands — are we comfortable with a short list of pilot nodes and the data redaction?

[16:24] Tom: yes, agreed.
[16:26] Lena: agreed.

[16:30] Maya: quick recap: Redwood will share the kv-verbose script and telemetry schema; Sable will run a 4-hr benchmark window and provide prompt set & traffic; Redwood will run the three-config benchmark; Diego will analyze and propose precise slab/prefetch params. next steps and action items will be in the deck.

[16:55] Diego: one more note: we spotted a subtle prefix-collision pattern in your logs where hashed prefixes from two different features collided in the same bucket because they use the same fingerprint salt — if you have feature flags pushing new prompts, rotate the salt during deployments.

[17:13] Priya: oh wow that explains a few odd collisions. we'll audit.

[17:20] Maya: ok let's finish with timeline and owners.
[17:23] Maya: Tom to collect logs and enable kv-verbose during the next mid-day peak by 2027-09-17. Diego to share trace script + bucket design doc by 2027-09-16. Priya to assemble prompt set and traffic profile by 2027-09-20. Maya to send pilot proposal and SLOs by 2027-09-18.

[17:48] Tom: noted. any final questions?
[17:51] Lena: no, thanks. very helpful.

[17:55] Diego: we'll upload an annotated example log and a short triage playbook to your shared drive. also linking the playbook: https://redwood.ai/kv-playbook (sample) — redacted for on-prem customers.

[18:08] Maya: great — thanks everyone, we'll follow up in the CRM with dates.

(End of recording)
